blocks.text: …make us leave before the inspector comes."
My partner kicked the door in. We didn't wait for police. The girl had said her mother was unconscious.

The woman who'd answered the door tried to block the stairs. My partner moved her aside. I ran up. In a back bedroom, a woman lay on the floor next to a space heater, barely breathing. The room smelled faintly sweet. My carbon monoxide detector, clipped to my belt, started screaming.

We carried the mother outside and gave her oxygen. Then we went back for the others. Three more people were in the house, a father and two teenage boys, all dizzy and sick. The little girl who called was nine. She'd felt sick too, gone to the kitchen for water, found her mother on the floor, and used an old landline in the hallway.
The mother spent two days in a hyperbaric chamber.

The county's records were right: the original house had burned in 2012. But someone rebuilt it, without permits, on the old foundation. The woman who answered the door was Darla Briggs, who owned the land. For years, she'd rented the house in cash to families who had nowhere else to go, mostly immigrants without legal status. She never fixed anything. The furnace was broken, so she provided space heaters. When tenants complained, she threatened to call immigration. She moved families in and out quickly so neighbors and inspectors wouldn't notice.
An inspector was scheduled to visit the property the next week after a neighbor complained. Darla had come that night to tell the family they had to be gone by morning.
When the girl's mother collapsed, Darla told the family not to call for help, because an ambulance would bring attention.
Darla was charged with reckless endangerment and housing violations. The family was placed in emergency housing and connected with an immigration attorney.

The little girl's name is Valeria. When I saw her at the hospital two days later, she asked me if her mom would be okay. I told her yes, because she'd been brave enough to call. She said, "The lady told us never to call anyone. But my mom says if someone stops breathing, you always call."
Every home should have a carbon monoxide detector. If yours doesn't, many local fire departments will install one for free.
